\chapter{Communication Complexity — Func Disjointness}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.CommunicationComplexity.DeterministicCC.FuncDisjointness
\section{Overview}

This module establishes the exact deterministic communication complexity of the
set-disjointness function on subsets of $[n]$.  Using a fooling-set argument based on
the pairs $(X, X^c)$, it shows that for $n \ge 1$ the complexity is exactly $n + 1$.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Set disjointness function]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness}
\statementsource{roughgarden-cc-bootcamp}{pdf-d54d402b16e2-p006-b001}
\statementsource{roughgarden-cc-oneway}{pdf-043896d6545f-p004-b002}
\statementsource{raoyehudayoff-ch01-deterministic-protocols}{pdf-fa052d8c95c0-p008-b005}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness}
\leanok
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and subsets $X, Y \subseteq [n]$, $\mathrm{disjointness}(n, X, Y)$
is the Boolean function that returns $\mathtt{true}$ if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are
disjoint, i.e.\ $X \cap Y = \emptyset$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetry of the set disjointness function]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness_comm}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness_comm}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness}
\difficulty{1}
For every $n \in \bbn$ and all subsets $X, Y \subseteq [n]$, the disjointness function
is symmetric in its two arguments: $\mathrm{disjointness}(n, X, Y) =
\mathrm{disjointness}(n, Y, X)$. That is, since $X$ and $Y$ are disjoint if and only if
$Y$ and $X$ are disjoint, swapping the two sets leaves the Boolean value unchanged.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Fooling set for disjointness]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet}
\statementsource{roughgarden-cc-bootcamp}{pdf-d54d402b16e2-p010-b005}
\statementsource{raoyehudayoff-ch01-deterministic-protocols}{pdf-fa052d8c95c0-p011-b007}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet}
\leanok
The candidate fooling set for disjointness is the collection of all pairs
$(X, X^c)$ where $X \subseteq [n]$, i.e.\ $\mathrm{foolingSet}(n) = \{(X, Y) \mid Y = X^c\}$.
\end{definition}

\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.foolingSet, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.IsFoolingSet, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.IsRectangle_iff}
\difficulty{5}
Fix $n \in \bbn$, and consider the set-disjointness function on subsets of $[n]$, namely
the Boolean function $g(X, Y)$ that is $\mathtt{true}$ exactly when $X \cap Y =
\emptyset$. Then the collection $\{(X, X^c) \mid X \subseteq [n]\}$ of complementary
pairs is a fooling set for $g$: for every rectangle $R = A \times B$ (with $A, B$
families of subsets of $[n]$) that is monochromatic for $g$, the intersection of $R$
with this collection contains at most one point.
\end{theorem}

\proofstep
  {CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness}
  {direct}
  {raoyehudayoff-ch01-deterministic-protocols}
  {pdf-fa052d8c95c0-p008-b005}
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity_le_clog_card_X_alpha, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Disjointness.disjointness}
\difficulty{3}
Fix $n \in \bbn$, and let both players' inputs range over subsets of $[n] = \{0, 1,
\dots, n-1\}$, so that Alice holds $X \subseteq [n]$ and Bob holds $Y \subseteq [n]$.
The deterministic communication complexity of the set-disjointness function, which
returns $\mathtt{true}$ exactly when $X \cap Y = \emptyset$, is at most $n + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{5}
Fix an integer $n \ge 1$, and consider the set-disjointness function on subsets of
$[n]$: it takes a pair of subsets $X, Y \subseteq [n]$ — Alice holding $X$ and Bob
holding $Y$ — to $\mathtt{true}$ exactly when $X \cap Y = \emptyset$. Then the
deterministic communication complexity of this function is at least $n + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{1}
Let $n \geq 1$, and let $\mathrm{disjointness}(n, \cdot, \cdot)$ denote the two-party
Boolean function that, given subsets $X, Y \subseteq [n]$ held by Alice and Bob
respectively, returns $\mathtt{true}$ exactly when $X \cap Y = \emptyset$. Then the
deterministic communication complexity of this function is exactly $n + 1$.
\end{theorem}
